title: De Fide Orthodoxa Contra Arianos
author: Ambrose

passages.original: — Videtis ergo omnia eos in tractatu ipsorum, non evangelica fide, sed subdola malignitate ad seducendos simplices quosque posuisse. Non jam tam suspectum, quam manifestum omnibus esse debet ita eos Deum de Deo posuisse, ut Arius tradere solebat ut ex Deo factus sit, non ex Deo natus. Qui si natus est, unius substantiæ est : si factus est, verus Filius non est: et si verus Filius non est, nec verus Deus est : aut si verus Deus est, et de Patre non est, duo sunt habentes singuli et voluntates proprias, et imperia diversa : vel si concordia tantum et societate unum sunt, non tamen et substantia verus, ut jam dixi, Deus non est.
passages.english: — You see, then, that in their treatise they have set down everything not in evangelical faith but with crafty malice, to lead astray all the simple. It ought now to be not so much suspected as plain to all that they have set down "God from God" in such a way as Arius used to teach, namely that he was made from God, not born from God. If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not a true Son; and if he is not a true Son, neither is he true God. Or if he is true God and is not from the Father, there are two, each having his own will and separate dominion. Or if they are one only by agreement and fellowship, and not also by substance, then, as I have already said, he is not true God.
passages.notes: "Not true God" is supplied for "verus ... Deus non est", which the edition splits across "non tamen et substantia verus, ut jam dixi, Deus non est"; "verus" seems displaced, and the sense taken is "if they are one only by concord, not also by substance, he is not, as I said, true God."

passages.original: Ita et Filium Dei similem volunt, ut eum aliunde similem, non de ipsa una sancta et beata Patris substantia dicant. Qui si de Patris substantia non est, ἐξ οὐϰ ὂντων est, id est, ex nullis exstantibus, ut idem Arius tradidit; sublato enim eo quod Pater est, undecumque fuerit Filius, necesse est ut et initium ex nihilo, et ortum ex tempore habeat: nibil enim sine initio, nisi solus Deus.'
passages.english: So too they want the Son of God to be "like", in such a way that they say he is like from some other source, not from the one holy and blessed substance of the Father itself. If he is not from the Father's substance, he is *ex ouk ontōn*, that is, from things not existing, as the same Arius taught. For once that which the Father is has been taken away, wherever the Son came from, he must have both a beginning from nothing and an origin in time. For nothing is without beginning except God alone.
passages.notes: "nibil" is a scanning error for "nihil"; the stray closing quotation mark at the end has been left out.
